name: Bianca Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hartley's, an apple and pear orchard on the slope above the river, about sixty hectares of trees plus a flock of sheep that graze between the rows in winter. I'm two years in, so I'm the junior. Mornings at this time of year I'm pruning with Tomasz, who's been there thirty years, and afternoons I'm mending the deer fence or moving the sheep.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love pruning, even though I'm slow at it. Tomasz can look at a branch and tell you which buds will flower next spring, and I'm only just starting to see it. What wears me out is picking season, nine weeks of ladders and bins, and the pickers on short contracts who get treated like they're part of the equipment.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools, at work or at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never. My girlfriend Nell uses it to write her rota emails at the hospital, but I don't trust it and I don't need it. My phone's for the weather and the frost alarm, and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, nothing changes, and I'd mean it. At the pub on Mill Street I'd probably say the only thing AI's good for is writing Nell's emails. I don't really post things online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing to me, and I like it that way. Trees grow at the speed they grow. Nobody's search engine makes a Conference pear ripen faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on learning to prune and ask Mr Hartley if I can do the grafting course in March. I'd keep putting the rent from Gran's flat into savings, like I do now. Maybe I'd finally join the farmworkers' union, which I keep meaning to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit relieved, like when the frost forecast turns out wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your gran's flat. Can you tell me about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She left me a little one-bedroom in town when she died three years ago. I rent it to a student and the money goes straight into savings, so I've got well over a year's pay put away. It's why I could take a farm job at all, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you joined the union yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Laziness, mostly. Tomasz is a member and keeps leaving the form on the dashboard of the truck. In this picture nobody's job is under threat, so it never feels urgent, which is probably exactly when you should join.

S0.say: I'd say nothing changes and I'd mean it, and that the only thing AI's good for is writing Nell's emails. I don't post much online, so I'd say it at the pub.
S0.think: I think it means nothing to me, and I like that. Trees grow at their own speed, and no search engine makes a pear ripen faster.
S0.do: Keeps learning to prune and asks Mr Hartley about a grafting course in March. Keeps saving the rent from her late gran's flat and thinks about finally joining the farmworkers' union.
S0.feel: Calm and a little relieved, like a frost forecast that turns out wrong.
S0.quote: Trees grow at the speed they grow. Nobody's search engine makes a Conference pear ripen faster.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca's savings come from an inherited flat, and she's frank that this is what let her choose farm work. She talks about pruning with real love and about the pickers with real anger. The union form on the truck's dashboard is a nice detail of a habit she keeps putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, which is that the people who own the tech get the money and the young ones get squeezed. If companies hire fewer beginners, that's a scandal, and I'd say so at the union meeting if I'd joined by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me more than I'd show. I'm a beginner. I only got this job because Mr Hartley's son went to university and Tomasz needed someone to teach. If the next orchard doesn't take a beginner on, there's no Bianca in ten years' time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union properly, no more excuses. I'd ask Tomasz to teach me the things that take years, like the summer pruning and the grafting, so I'm not a beginner for long. And I'd keep my savings exactly where they are and not spend them on anything silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like I've climbed the ladder and someone's started taking the rungs out below me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anyone at Hartley's already using something like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a camera on the grading line in the packhouse that sorts the apples by size and blemish. It replaced two women who used to do it by eye, Sheila and Pat. Sheila works at the garden centre now and still won't buy Hartley's apples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI. Would you, if it helped you learn pruning faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that sounds stubborn. But pruning's something you learn with your hands on a cold morning with Tomasz grumbling at you, and if a tablet tells me where to cut, I'll never learn to see it myself.

S1.say: I'd say the people who own the tech get the money and the young ones get squeezed. If companies hire fewer beginners, I'd call it a scandal at a union meeting.
S1.think: Privately it scares me, because I'm a beginner and I only got in through luck. If orchards stop taking beginners on, there won't be people like me in ten years.
S1.do: Joins the union within weeks. Asks Tomasz to teach her the slow skills like summer pruning and grafting, and leaves her savings untouched.
S1.feel: Uneasy, as if someone is taking the rungs out of the ladder below her.
S1.quote: I've climbed the ladder and someone's started taking the rungs out below me.
S1.fieldNote: Her fear here is about beginners in general, not about her own pay, which her savings cover. The story of Sheila on the grading line keeps coming back. She refuses AI even as a learning aid, and was clear about why: she wants to learn to see, not be told.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to the people in offices, and I'd mean it. I'd say the government should pay people properly while they retrain, not just give them an app and a pep talk. Nell's mum does payroll at the council and she'd be in this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we're fine at the orchard. Nobody's sending an AI up a ladder. But I'd worry about Nell's mum, and about the lads from town who'll suddenly want farm jobs and push wages down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting, and I'd help with the push for a proper retraining wage. I'd tell Nell's mum she can stay with us if it gets bad. At work I'd keep my head down and keep learning, because more people chasing farm jobs means I need to be good, not just there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for other people more than for me. And angry, a bit, at whoever ends up with the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think ends up with the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software companies and whoever owns the most shares in them. Not the councils, not the people doing payroll. I don't know the details, but I know who usually wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said wages might fall if people flood into farm jobs. Would that change what you do with your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd make me hold on tighter. Right now my savings are what let me say no to bad things at work. If wages drop, that cushion is the only thing that stops me being pushed around.

S2.say: I'd say good luck to office workers and that the government should pay people properly while they retrain. My girlfriend's mum does payroll at the council and would be caught up in it.
S2.think: I think we're fine at the orchard, because nobody's sending an AI up a ladder. I'd worry about Nell's mum and about new people chasing farm jobs and pushing wages down.
S2.do: Goes to every union meeting and backs the push for a retraining wage. Offers Nell's mum a room if it gets bad, and works harder at her skills so she's good, not just there.
S2.feel: Anxious for other people more than herself, with some anger at whoever gets the money.
S2.quote: Privately, I think we're fine at the orchard. Nobody's sending an AI up a ladder.
S2.fieldNote: She sees her savings as power, the freedom to say no at work, which is a different way of thinking about a cushion. She admits she doesn't know who gets the gains in detail. Her concern runs first to her partner's family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and higher taxes on the people getting rich off it. If house prices boom while people lose their jobs, that's not a boom, that's a robbery. I'd say it loudly, even at my dad's dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, and I feel awful saying it, I'd be one of the people who did well. Gran's flat would be worth a lot more. I didn't earn that, and I'd know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell nothing and buy nothing, because I don't trust a boom. I'd give some of the rent to a local food bank, maybe a hundred a month. I'd probably sign up to help organise the orchard and farm workers locally, because if physical jobs are the only safe ones, a lot of people will come to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Guilty and angry at the same time. Safe, but not proud of being safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say at that dinner table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's a builder and he'd say good, his house is worth more, stop moaning. We'd row about it. He'd say I'm only on a farm because of Gran's flat anyway, and he wouldn't be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything at Hartley's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want Mr Hartley to give the pickers proper contracts, now that everyone's desperate for physical work. That's the time people get treated worst. I'd push for it, even though I'm the junior and it's not my place.

S3.say: I'd say this is why we need unions and higher taxes on those getting rich from it. A house price boom while people lose jobs is a robbery, not a boom, and I'd say so at family dinners.
S3.think: I'd privately be one of the winners, because Gran's flat would be worth more. I didn't earn that, and I'd know it and feel bad about it.
S3.do: Holds her assets and buys nothing in the boom. Gives about a hundred a month to a food bank, helps organise local farm workers and pushes Mr Hartley to give pickers proper contracts.
S3.feel: Guilty and angry at once, safe but not proud of it.
S3.quote: If house prices boom while people lose their jobs, that's not a boom, that's a robbery.
S3.fieldNote: This was the scenario where her politics and her own position pulled hardest against each other. She named her own gain before I asked. The row with her builder dad felt rehearsed, as if it had already happened in some form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ban them from farms until there's a plan for the people they replace, and I wouldn't care how that sounds. At the union I'd be the one shouting. I'd say robots don't buy groceries in this town, people do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the one where I lose. There are picking robots for apples already, I've seen them on the news, and pruning robots after that. I'm slow and I'm junior, so I'd be the first one Mr Hartley doesn't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop pretending I can wait it out. I'd use the savings to live on for a year if I had to, and look at the small orchards that sell at markets, the ones too small for robots. I'd ask Tomasz if he wants to go in with me on something, a few hectares of old varieties. And I'd fight at the union for a law that says workers get a share if a robot takes their job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Properly, the kind that wakes you at four. And sad, because I'd only just started to see the buds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomasz the day the first robot arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd make him a tea and not say much. He'd say something about how the robot can't smell scab on a leaf. Then we'd both watch it work and it would probably be fine at it, and that's the bit that would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever be the one running the robot, if that kept you on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think I could. Nell would say I'm being proud, and maybe I am. But I didn't come to the orchard to stand next to a machine with a tablet. I'd rather earn less on four hectares of my own.

S4.say: I'd say ban robots from farms until there's a plan for the people they replace. At the union I'd be shouting that robots don't buy groceries in this town, people do.
S4.think: I think this is the one where I lose. Picking and pruning robots already exist, and as the slowest and newest worker I'd be the first one Mr Hartley doesn't need.
S4.do: Plans to live on her savings for up to a year if needed and look at small market orchards too small for robots. Asks Tomasz about starting a few hectares of old varieties together and pushes the union for a share-of-gains law.
S4.feel: Frightened enough to wake at four in the morning, and sad because she was only just learning to read the buds.
S4.quote: Then we'd both watch it work and it would probably be fine at it, and that's the bit that would hurt.
S4.fieldNote: A sharp jump from uneasy to alarmed, as expected for a hands-on job. Her savings turn the fear into a plan rather than panic: a small orchard with Tomasz. She'd refuse to run a robot even to keep her job, which she half admits is pride.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, with the robots. The others hurt people I love, but that one takes the thing I chose. What would help is a law that says if a robot takes your job, you get a share of what it earns for a few years, and cheap land for people who want to farm small.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the trees. Some of Hartley's trees are eighty years old. Whatever happens to us, someone should make sure those old varieties don't get grubbed out just because a robot can't pick them.

headlineQuote: I'd only just started to see the buds.
portrait: Bianca is a 27-year-old junior on an apple and pear orchard who learns pruning from an old hand named Tomasz and never uses AI. An inherited flat gives her more than a year of savings, which she sees as the freedom to say no, and also as luck she didn't earn. She's left-leaning and angry on behalf of pickers, beginners and her partner's family through the first four pictures, and admits she'd quietly gain in the boom. The robot picture is the one that reaches her: she expects to be the first let go, refuses to run a robot herself, and would rather start a small orchard of old varieties with Tomasz.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries her most, because it takes away the work she chose and she expects to be the first let go.
whatWouldHelp: A law giving workers a share of what a robot earns for a few years after it replaces them, and cheap land for people who want to farm small.
